items.prompt: Private waste collectors in Katutura serve the households that pay and skip the lanes of those that do not, so uncollected waste piles up across the neighbourhood. Define market failure as the term applies to this market for waste collection.
items.canonical_answer: Market failure is the failure of the price mechanism, left to itself, to allocate resources in the way that best serves society. Here collectors serve only paying households, so the harm of uncollected waste falls on the whole neighbourhood and collection is under-provided.
marking_guidance: Reward the precise definition: the price mechanism allocating resources against society's interest, because the price leaves some costs or benefits uncounted.
The meaning must rest on the whole market's level of output; a definition resting on firms closing describes business failure, not market failure.

items.prompt: Namib Signs proposes to fund a new beam of lighting over Otavi's main taxi rank from a voluntary levy, and drivers who refuse to pay would still see by its light. Identify the features that make this lighting a public good.
items.canonical_answer: The lighting is non-excludable, since drivers who refuse the levy cannot be stopped from seeing by the beam, and non-rival, since one driver's use leaves as much light for the next. Together these invite free riding, so a voluntary levy tends to raise too little.
marking_guidance: Reward the features named - non-excludability and non-rivalry - with the free-rider consequence each leads to.
What it includes: each feature must be explained in the case's own terms, not merely listed - a bare word earns nothing.

items.prompt: Otavi Charcoal Works burns wood waste for N$40 000 of income a season, and the smoke over 60 homesteads costs each N$250 in cleaning and clinic visits. Define an external cost as the term applies to this case.
items.canonical_answer: An external cost is a cost an activity imposes on people outside the transaction, who receive no payment for it. Here it is the N$250 each of the 60 homesteads spends on cleaning and clinic visits, which the charcoal works never pays.
marking_guidance: Reward the precise definition: a cost imposed on third parties outside the transaction, for which they receive no payment.
The meaning must separate external costs from private costs; a definition that counts the firm's own spending as external earns nothing.

items.prompt: Oshakati Textiles dyes cloth for N$90 000 of sales a month. Its dye water runs into the town channel, and 20 market gardens downstream each lose N$1 500 a month of crops. Analyse the consequences of this market failure for the firm's owners, the market gardeners, and the town's council.
items.canonical_answer: The dye water pushes costs onto people outside the firm's transactions: 20 gardens each lose N$1 500 a month, so 20 x N$1 500 = N$30 000 a month. Because the price of dyed cloth carries none of this, the firm's costs understate the true cost to society, and the market dyes more cloth than Oshakati as a whole would choose. The owners gain, because profit measured against private costs alone makes the dye house look more profitable than it is for the town. The 20 market gardeners each lose N$1 500 of crops a month with no compensation. The council faces either the clean-up bill for the channel or the loss of the gardens' produce.
marking_guidance: Starting point: the initial change - the dye water entering the channel - must be named first, with the N$30 000 attached.
Mechanism: because the price carries none of the costs imposed on others, this causes output above the level society would choose.
Consequence: therefore each named party - the owners, the market gardeners, the council - needs its own traced outcome; N$1 500 a garden is the evidence.
For whom: state for whom each consequence lands - the owner, the gardener, the council.

items.prompt: Ruacana Radio reaches 80 000 listeners across the Kunene region, and a season of broadcasts costs N$90 000 to run. A listener with a radio tunes in whether or not they have paid, and one listener tuning in leaves the signal as strong for the next. Explain, for this market, why these two features cause private broadcasters to provide too little air time.
items.canonical_answer: The signal is non-excludable, because anyone with a radio can tune in without paying, and non-rival, because one listener leaves the signal as strong for the next. Since non-payers get the full benefit, each listener is likely to wait for others to pay - the free-rider problem. A private broadcaster therefore struggles to collect enough from the 80 000 listeners to cover the N$90 000 a season, so it provides less air time than listeners would value: the market under-provides.
marking_guidance: The context - the two features and the figures - must anchor the answer: non-excludability and non-rivalry, drawn from the prompt.
Reasoning: because non-payers benefit regardless, the link is the free-rider problem - each listener waiting for others to pay.
Conclusion: therefore the market under-provides air time relative to the region's gain, and that shortfall is the market failure.

items.prompt: Cheap strong brew sells 2 200 cartons a month in Swakopmund while the town clinic judges 1 500 the manageable level. Define over-consumption as a consequence of market failure, using these figures.
items.canonical_answer: Over-consumption is consumption above the level that matches a good's full social costs. Here 2 200 cartons a month are bought against a manageable 1 500, so 2 200 - 1 500 = 700 cartons too many, because the price ignores the harm to others.
marking_guidance: Reward the precise definition: consumption above the level that matches the good's full social costs, with the figures attached.
The meaning must tie the excess to the price failing to carry the good's costs to others; a definition of buying more than before earns nothing.

items.prompt: The Oshakati clinic sells flu vaccinations at N$60 each and 300 are bought in a season. The clinic estimates that the level serving the whole town - counting the protection each vaccination gives to the neighbours of the person vaccinated - is 900 a season. Discuss whether the market for vaccinations in Oshakati is failing, and what the shortfall means for the town.
items.canonical_answer: Buyers decide at N$60 by weighing the protection they themselves receive. Each vaccination also protects classmates, neighbours and people in the taxi queue, but that external benefit enters no buyer's decision, so the market settles at 300 a season against the 900 the clinic judges would serve the town - a shortfall of 900 - 300 = 600 vaccinations. The link is that the price mechanism counts private benefit alone, so a merit good with external benefits is under-consumed. The consequence lands on the unvaccinated: flu spreads further than it needs to, households lose work and school days, and the clinic treats cases vaccination could have prevented. Against this, the 900 is the clinic's own estimate rather than an observed figure, and some people may refuse vaccination for reasons a lower price would not change, so the true shortfall may be smaller. On balance the market is failing: even if the estimate is generous, the benefits to others are real and the price ignores them.
marking_guidance: The link: the price counts only the buyer's own protection, so the benefit to neighbours is left out and the market settles at 300 rather than 900.
The consequence: 600 vaccinations a season under-consumed, landing on the unvaccinated neighbours, their households and the clinic.
A Discuss answer weighs a limit - the 900 is an estimate, and some refusals are not about price - and reaches a judgement on whether the market is failing.

items.prompt: A Katutura clinic keeps two seasons of records for a sugary soft drink sold at the same N$6 a bottle throughout. Season 1: 8 000 bottles sold, 90 dental cases. Season 2: 12 000 bottles sold, 210 dental cases. Explain what these figures show about the over-consumption of the drink.
items.canonical_answer: Bottles sold and dental cases rise together: bottles from 8 000 to 12 000 while cases climb from 90 to 210. The price stays at N$6, yet the clinic hours and missed school the sugar causes never enter it, so buyers face a cheaper choice than society bears and consumption rises above the level society would choose. However, two seasons cannot prove the drink alone caused the cases - diets and brushing habits may have changed - and the level society would choose is estimated, not observed.
marking_guidance: What the data shows - the positive relationship between bottles sold and dental cases - must be stated first, with the supporting evidence taken as a comparison across the two seasons.
The exception or caution earns a mark: however, two seasons cannot separate the drink's effect from other changes, and the social level is an estimate.
The why - an explanation of the relationship, through the price carrying none of the costs to others - is the core mark; quoting the bottles alone is not interpretation.

items.prompt: Enrolment at Ruacana's evening book-keeping classes stands at 200 students a term at a fee of N$50, while the region's employers judge 600 the level their payrolls need, and families undervalue the classes' later payoff. Explain, for this town, the consequences of this under-consumption for the students who stayed away, the employers, and the wider economy.
items.canonical_answer: Enrolment is 200 against the 600 employers need, a shortfall of 600 - 200 = 400 students a term at an unchanged N$50 fee. Because families undervalue the classes' later payoff - book-keeping training is a merit good - demand sits below the level its full benefits justify. Therefore 400 potential book-keepers a term miss the skill and the earnings it brings, employers face vacancies they cannot fill locally, and the wider economy builds less skill than it could.
marking_guidance: The context - 200 enrolled against 600 needed, at the unchanged N$50 - must anchor the answer; the figures are the evidence.
Reasoning: because families undervalue a merit good, the link is demand below the level the classes' full benefits would justify.
Conclusion: therefore name what the shortfall of 400 students a term costs the students who stayed away, the employers and the wider economy.

items.prompt: A tobacco stall at Oshakati's open market sells 3 500 packs of cigarettes a month at N$30 a pack. The state clinic spends N$400 000 a month treating the chest cases that follow, and judges 2 000 packs a month the level its wards could manage. Analyse the consequences of this over-consumption for the smokers, their households, and the state clinic.
items.canonical_answer: The stall sells 3 500 packs a month against the 2 000 the clinic judges manageable, so 3 500 - 2 000 = 1 500 packs too many. Because the N$30 price carries none of the N$400 000 the clinic spends each month, a pack looks cheaper to the smoker than it is to society, so consumption of this demerit good settles above the manageable level. Smokers bear health damage the price did not signal. Their households lose income and care hours to treatment, taken from school fees and food. The clinic spends N$400 000 a month on these cases, which crowds out its other patients, so the misallocation lands on all three.
marking_guidance: Starting point: the initial change - 3 500 packs against the 2 000 judged manageable - must be named first, with the 1 500-pack gap attached.
Mechanism: because the price carries none of the clinic's costs, this causes consumption above the level society would choose - the demerit-good failure.
Consequence: therefore each named party - the smokers, the households, the clinic - needs its own traced outcome; N$400 000 a month is the evidence.
For whom: name for whom each consequence lands - the smoker, the household, the clinic's other patients.

items.prompt: Define a merit good, as the term is used when explaining why some goods are under-consumed.
items.canonical_answer: A merit good is a good whose benefits consumers tend to undervalue, so that, left to the market, it is under-consumed. Schooling and vaccination are examples.
marking_guidance: Precise meaning: the definition must state that consumers tend to undervalue the good's benefits, and that as a result the market tends to leave it under-consumed.
An example such as schooling or vaccination supports the meaning but does not replace it; a good whose harm consumers undercount is a demerit good, the opposite term.

items.prompt: Define a demerit good, as the term is used when explaining why some goods are over-consumed.
items.canonical_answer: A demerit good is a good whose harm consumers tend to undercount, so that, left to the market, it is over-consumed. Tobacco and strong drink are examples.
marking_guidance: Precise meaning: the definition must state that consumers tend to undercount the harm the good does, and that as a result the market tends to leave it over-consumed.
An example such as tobacco or strong drink supports the meaning but does not replace it; a good whose benefits consumers undervalue is a merit good, the opposite term.

items.prompt: Define a private cost.
items.canonical_answer: A private cost is a cost paid directly by the person or firm that decides to produce or consume a good, such as the diesel a bus operator buys to run its buses.
marking_guidance: Precise meaning: the definition must state that the cost is paid by the decision-maker itself - the producer or consumer in the transaction.
A cost that falls on people outside the transaction is an external cost and is not credited as a private cost.

items.prompt: Omaruru Brickworks pays N$6 000 a week for clay, fuel and wages. Smoke from its kilns costs nearby farms an estimated N$2 500 a week in cleaning and damaged crops. Calculate the weekly social cost of the brickworks' production.
items.canonical_answer: Social cost = private cost + external cost. N$6 000 + N$2 500 = N$8 500 a week.
marking_guidance: Formula: social cost = private cost + external cost.
Substitution: the working puts the N$6 000 private cost and the N$2 500 external cost into the formula.
Answer with units: N$8 500 a week. N$2 500 alone is the external cost, not the social cost.

items.prompt: Define a private benefit.
items.canonical_answer: A private benefit is a benefit received by the person who buys or consumes a good, such as the cleaner yard a household gains when it connects to the town sewer.
marking_guidance: Precise meaning: the definition must state that the benefit goes to the buyer or consumer in the transaction itself.
A benefit that goes to people outside the transaction is an external benefit and is not credited as a private benefit.

items.prompt: Define social benefit.
items.canonical_answer: Social benefit is the total benefit of an activity to society: the private benefit to the buyer plus the external benefit to people outside the transaction.
marking_guidance: Precise meaning: the definition must give social benefit as the total, naming both parts - private benefit plus external benefit.
External benefit alone is only the part that reaches people outside the transaction, so it is not credited as social benefit.

items.prompt: Nami Bus Lines holds the single licence to run buses between Rundu and Katima Mulilo, and no other operator may enter the route. It has raised the fare from N$180 to N$240 and cut daily departures from six to four. Explain how this abuse of monopoly power is a cause of market failure.
items.canonical_answer: The context shows a seller with no rival: no other operator may enter, so passengers cannot switch. Because of this, Nami Bus Lines can raise the fare by N$240 - N$180 = N$60 and cut departures from six to four without losing passengers to a competitor. Fewer trips run, and each costs more than rivals would allow. Therefore travel on the route is under-provided: resources are misallocated away from what passengers want, which means the market has failed.
marking_guidance: Context: the answer must use the data - the single licence, the fare rise from N$180 to N$240 and the cut from six to four departures.
Reasoning: the because link must be written out - with no rival, buyers cannot switch, so the seller can raise its price and restrict output.
Conclusion: therefore output sits below what society wants and resources are misallocated, which means the market has failed.

items.prompt: Oshana Milling is the single maize miller supplying shops in northern Namibia, protected by the high cost of building a mill. It cuts output from 50 000 to 40 000 bags a month and raises the price from N$110 to N$140 a bag. Analyse the consequences of this abuse of monopoly power for consumers, the miller and the economy.
items.canonical_answer: When Oshana Milling cuts output and raises its price, buyers cannot switch, because the cost of building a mill keeps rivals out. This causes monthly revenue to move from N$110 x 50 000 = N$5 500 000 to N$140 x 40 000 = N$5 600 000 while the mill grinds less, so its costs are likely to fall and its profit to rise. Consumers pay N$30 more a bag and 10 000 fewer bags reach households, which hits low-income families hardest because maize meal is a staple. For the economy, fewer resources go into milling than buyers want, so resources are misallocated and the market has failed.
marking_guidance: Starting point: the initial change - output cut from 50 000 to 40 000 bags and the price raised from N$110 to N$140 - is named first.
Mechanism: because barriers keep rivals out, buyers cannot switch; this causes revenue and profit to rise while output falls.
Consequence: therefore consumers pay N$30 more a bag, 10 000 fewer bags are sold and resources are misallocated.
For whom: each consequence is placed on the consumer, the firm and the economy.

items.prompt: When Ombili Copper's mine near Tsumeb closes, 400 miners lose their jobs. In the same month, building firms in Windhoek report 250 unfilled posts for bricklayers and electricians. Explain how factor immobility causes market failure in this case.
items.canonical_answer: The data shows labour idle in one place and needed in another: 400 miners out of work near Tsumeb while 250 building posts stay empty in Windhoek. Because the miners' skills do not match bricklaying or electrical work, and homes and families tie them to Tsumeb, they cannot move into the vacant posts quickly. This means labour sits unused while building work goes undone, so resources are not allocated to where they are wanted, which is market failure.
marking_guidance: Context: the answer must use the data - 400 miners out of work near Tsumeb and 250 unfilled building posts in Windhoek.
Reasoning: the because link must be written out - skills that do not transfer and ties of home and family stop labour moving to the new use.
Conclusion: therefore labour stays unused where it is not needed while needs go unmet elsewhere, which means resources are misallocated.

items.prompt:
Eight questions in the style of Paper 1. Choose one option for each.

1. Market failure is best defined as:
A  a firm closing because it cannot cover its costs
B  the price mechanism allocating resources in a way that does not best serve society
C  a government refusing to intervene in markets
D  a shortage of goods at the current price

2. A cost imposed on people outside a transaction, for which they receive no payment, is:
A  a private cost
B  an external cost
C  a social benefit
D  a cost of production

3. Street lighting over Katutura's taxi ranks is a public good because it is:
A  excludable and rival
B  free to produce
C  non-excludable and non-rival
D  owned by the council

4. A merit good is:
A  one whose benefits consumers tend to undervalue
B  one the government bans
C  one whose use harms others directly
D  one sold below the cost of producing it

5. Because those who pay nothing still benefit, public goods tend to be:
A  over-provided by private firms
B  under-provided by private firms
C  provided at the level society would choose
D  priced out of most households' reach

6. Which is a demerit good?
A  childhood vaccination
B  schooling
C  tobacco
D  street lighting

7. The social cost of an activity is:
A  its private costs alone
B  its external costs alone
C  its private costs plus its external costs
D  its price multiplied by its quantity

8. Over-consumption of a good with external costs happens because:
A  the price carries none of the costs the good imposes on others
B  consumers cannot afford the good
C  the good is a public good
D  the government subsidises the good
items.canonical_answer:
Key: 1 B, 2 B, 3 C, 4 A, 5 B, 6 C, 7 C, 8 A.
1. B is the definition - a whole market misallocating resources. A confuses market failure with business failure; C names a policy stance, not a market outcome; D names a shortage at one price, which a moving price tends to correct.
2. B: external costs fall on third parties unpaid. A counts the payer's own costs; C names a benefit, not a cost; D names a firm's accounting cost, not a cost imposed outside it.
3. C: non-excludable - non-payers cannot be stopped from benefiting - and non-rival - one user's use leaves as much for the next. A reverses both features; B confuses a public good with a free good, which is naturally abundant rather than costly to provide; D confuses ownership with the two defining features.
4. A: a merit good is undervalued by its own consumers, so too little is bought. B confuses a merit good with a banned good; C describes a good imposing external costs; D confuses undervaluing with a price below cost.
5. B: the free-rider problem withdraws private provision. A reverses the direction; C assumes the market finds the social level, which the missing payments prevent; D mistakes a funding shortfall for a high-price problem.
6. C: tobacco is consumed above the level its harm to others would justify. A and B are merit goods, undervalued by consumers; D is a public good, under-provided for a different reason.
7. C: social costs combine what the decision-maker pays and what third parties bear. A omits the external costs; B omits the private costs; D computes revenue, not cost.
8. A: with part of the cost left unpaid by buyers, the market level sits above the social level. B would lower consumption, not raise it; C names a different cause, of under-provision; D names a remedy that lowers consumption rather than raising it.
marking_guidance: Key: one mark per question, eight in total; the correct option for each is listed and every distractor is explained as the specific misunderstanding it catches.

Each distractor traces to a named error: market failure confused with business failure, external costs confused with private costs, a public good confused with a free good, merit goods confused with demerit goods, social costs confused with revenue, and a cause confused with a remedy.

items.prompt:
A radio report from Walvis Bay, March 2027: "Pelagic Processors opened its second fish-meal line this year. The plant's washings drain through the town channel into the lagoon. Net fishers say their season's catch is down; the plant says its processing volume is up. The town council has published its first lagoon survey."

Table 1 - Pelagic Processors, Walvis Bay
  fish-meal output: 900 tonnes last year, 1 500 tonnes this year
  washings drained per tonne processed: 4 litres
  net fishers affected: 30, each losing N$2 000 of catch a season
  council dredging estimate: N$500 000

(a) Calculate the litres of washings drained this year. [1]
(b) Identify from Table 1 two costs the plant's price does not carry. [2]
(c) Explain why the market produces more fish-meal than the level Walvis Bay as a whole would choose. [4]
(d) Analyse what the survey suggests for the plant's owners, the net fishers and the council, using the data as evidence. [6]
items.canonical_answer:
(a) 1 500 x 4 = 6 000 litres of washings this year.
(b) The net fishers' lost catch - N$2 000 each across 30 fishers - and the council's N$500 000 dredging estimate, one mark each: both are costs imposed on parties outside the plant's transactions, and the price of fish-meal carries neither.
(c) The washings impose costs on the fishers and the council that the price of fish-meal does not carry, so the plant's private costs understate the activity's social costs. Because buyers pay a price set against private costs alone, the market settles at 1 500 tonnes, above the level that would match the full costs to the town; this is over-production, and the second production line shows the market extending an activity whose full costs it never reads.
(d) Processing volume rises with the waste the lagoon absorbs, so the harm and the output move together. Output rose from 900 to 1 500 tonnes, washings ran at 6 000 litres this year, and 30 fishers lost N$60 000 of catch between them, since 30 x N$2 000 = N$60 000, beside a N$500 000 dredging estimate. For the owners, the second line adds revenue judged against private costs alone, so expansion looks more profitable than it is for the town; for the fishers, N$60 000 of income is lost to a plant whose price they never set; for the council, N$500 000 of dredging competes with other spending plans. However, the catch fall may owe something to weather and stock movements a first survey cannot separate, and the dredging estimate is a single survey's figure rather than a settled cost.
marking_guidance: Parts (a) and (b) are read from the data; the six-mark part must use the figures as evidence - the tonnage rise, the 6 000 litres, the N$60 000 of lost catch, the N$500 000 dredging estimate - not as analysis itself.
One mark per distinct linked statement in (c): the costs the price does not carry, and the market level sitting above the social level, carry the marks.
Part (d) is marked on expected relationship, then evidence, then analysis, then an exception; quoting figures without the relationship they support earns nothing.
For whom: consequences must be named for the plant's owners, the net fishers and the council, each with its own traced outcome.

facts: 30 net fishers each lose N$2 000 a season

items.prompt:
Gobabis households use the services of one health trust and one high school. Answer all parts.

(a) Define market failure. [2]
(b) Explain the difference between a merit good and a demerit good, and say which way each is misallocated. [4]
(c) The Gobabis health trust sells child vaccinations at N$45 each and 400 are bought a season; the trust judges 1 000 the level that would protect the town. Analyse what this shortfall means for the town's children, their families and the trust. [6]
(d) Discuss whether selling a merit good at a price low enough for the town's households to meet would end its under-consumption. [8]
items.canonical_answer:
(a) Market failure is the failure of the price mechanism to allocate resources in the way that best serves society, so the market produces too much of some goods and too little of others relative to the levels that would match their full costs and benefits.
(b) A merit good is one whose benefits consumers tend to undervalue, so the market under-consumes it - vaccination, schooling. A demerit good is one whose harm consumers tend to undercount, so the market over-consumes it - tobacco, strong drink. The two are misallocated in opposite directions: resources sit behind too little of the merit good and too much of the demerit good, in each case because the price carries less of the good's full effects than society bears.
(c) The market buys 400 vaccinations against a protective level of 1 000, a shortfall of 600, since 1 000 - 400 = 600 vaccinations, at an unchanged price of N$45. Because buyers count the protection their own children receive and skip the protection a vaccinated child gives to classmates and neighbours, demand at N$45 sits below where the good's social benefits would place it. For the children, 600 remain exposed to a disease the vaccine checks. For their families, that exposure brings the risk of treatment costs and lost school days. For the trust, capacity flows into treating the cases the price did not prevent. The shortfall is therefore carried by the unprotected children, their families and the ward's other patients.
(d) The case for is that a lower price moves buyers down the demand curve, so the quantity demanded rises; where the barrier was ability to pay, an affordable price removes it, and the quantity moves towards the protective level. The case against is that where the barrier is undervaluing rather than affordability - families who doubt the vaccine, or weigh today's N$45 against other needs - a lower price does nothing to change what the good looks worth in their eyes, so demand may still sit below the social level; and the trust must cover the cost of production from somewhere, which may require the council's budget or a donor. On balance, an affordable price narrows the shortfall where ability to pay is the binding constraint; it ends under-consumption provided the undervaluing has also been addressed, and the condition it depends on is whether the trust's costs can be covered at that price, and whether the families who stayed away were priced out or unconvinced.
marking_guidance: Every part carries a model answer; part (d) is level-marked over three bands.
(a) rewards the precise definition: the price mechanism allocating against society's interest, not a single firm's fortunes.
(b) one mark per distinct point: undervaluing against undercounting, under-consumption against over-consumption, each with the link made.
(c) one mark per distinct linked statement from the starting point - the 600-vaccination shortfall at an unchanged price - through the mechanism to the consequence for each named party.

(d) Level 3 examines why it might - affordability lifting the quantity demanded - and why it might not - undervaluing left untouched, and the cost of provision - and reaches a judgement naming the condition it depends on; Level 2 develops one side; Level 1 asserts.

items.prompt: Plan an answer to: "The council proposes a N$5 tax on each carton of strong brew sold in Swakopmund, where 2 200 cartons a month are sold against the 1 500 the clinic judges manageable. Discuss whether a tax is the best way to correct this over-consumption." Do not write the essay; produce the plan.
items.canonical_answer:
Case for: the tax makes the brew's price carry part of the cost its use imposes on the clinic, so the price the buyer faces moves closer to the activity's full cost.
Chain 1: the tax raises the price -> buying becomes dearer at each quantity -> the quantity demanded tends to fall -> consumption moves towards the manageable level (for the town's health service).
Case against, first point: where the habit keeps buyers paying, the quantity demanded may fall very little, and the tax raises revenue without moving the level much.
Chain 2: the tax raises the price -> buyers with few alternatives keep buying -> the quantity stays near 2 200 cartons -> the over-consumption persists and the tax weighs on household budgets (for the drinker's family).
Case against, second point: a tax works through the price alone, while education, age checks and clinic outreach work on the undervaluing itself, and unrecorded sellers may trade outside the tax.
Chain 3: the tax reaches recorded sales -> unrecorded sellers take the trade -> the taxed market shrinks while the total sold may not -> the correction falls short of the whole market (for the council).
Judgement: a tax is likely to move the level towards 1 500 cartons where buyers respond to price and the recorded market covers the sales; the condition it depends on is how strongly the quantity demanded answers the price, and whether the council can enforce the tax across the sellers.
marking_guidance: A plan, not an essay: the structure with the stated judgement is what is assessed.
The plan must carry the case for and the case against, each developed as a chain from the tax to its consequence, and name the parties - the health service, the drinker's family, the council.
The judgement must be decisive and name the condition it depends on: how strongly quantity demanded answers the price, and whether the tax reaches the unrecorded sellers.
What settles it: whether the price change moves the quantity or merely moves revenue - the decisive test is the response of the quantity demanded.
